name: Certified Implementation Specialist – Risk and Compliance
note: ServiceNow does not publish a cut score for CIS-RC; community consensus puts it near 70%. Treat 85% here as your readiness bar. Items marked release-sensitive reference table names and labels that shift between releases; verify them against your own instance.

questions.stem: What most distinguishes integrated risk management (IRM) from a traditional, siloed GRC program?
options: IRM replaces internal audit with automated control testing so assurance no longer depends on people
IRM concentrates on regulatory compliance and leaves enterprise risk decisions to each business unit
IRM ties risk, compliance, and audit to shared data and live operational records for continuous monitoring
IRM gives each line of defense its own dedicated platform so their data never overlaps or conflicts
questions.explanation:
The defining shift is integration: one data model, shared entities, and direct links to operational records such as CIs, changes, and incidents. That is what lets controls be monitored continuously instead of sampled once a year in spreadsheets.

IRM supports internal audit rather than replacing it. It covers enterprise risk as much as compliance. And the whole point is one platform across the lines of defense, not one per line.

questions.stem: A compliance team maps a single internal control objective to requirements in ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, and PCI DSS. What business benefit does this illustrate?
options: Test once, comply many: one control is evaluated and the result counts toward each mapped regulation
Auditors can skip testing any control that maps to more than one regulation because it is pre-validated
Once a control exists, the mapped regulations no longer need to be monitored for future changes
Each regulation gets its own independent control set so auditors can trace every requirement cleanly
questions.explanation:
Mapping overlapping requirements to a common internal control means the organization tests and evidences that control once, and the result rolls up to every authority document it satisfies. That is the main cost driver IRM programs attack.

Separate control sets per regulation multiply testing effort. Regulations still change and must be tracked. Auditors still test mapped controls — the efficiency is in not testing the same thing three times.

questions.stem: Under the three lines model, which function is the third line?
options: External regulators
Internal audit, which provides independent assurance
The risk and compliance function that sets frameworks and oversees the first line
Operational management that owns and manages risk day to day
questions.explanation:
The first line owns and manages risk in operations, the second line (risk management, compliance) sets frameworks and provides oversight, and the third line (internal audit) provides independent assurance to the board.

Regulators and external auditors sit outside the model. The exam uses this to test which ServiceNow persona maps to which line — audit managers are the third line.

questions.stem: In ServiceNow IRM terminology, what is the difference between a risk and an issue?
options: A risk is a potential event that could affect objectives; an issue is a known gap that needs remediation
They are the same underlying record, presented differently in the risk and compliance applications
A risk is raised by internal auditors during fieldwork; an issue is raised by second-line risk managers
An issue is simply a risk that has been formally accepted, approved, and closed by its risk owner
questions.explanation:
Risk is forward-looking — something that might happen. An issue is a known gap now: a failed control, a non-compliant attestation, an audit finding. Issues carry owners and remediation plans.

Either can come from any function. They are distinct records. Accepting a risk is a risk response, not a conversion into an issue.

questions.stem: Why does running IRM on the same platform as ITSM, ITOM, and the CMDB matter to a compliance program?
options: Controls and risks can reference the same CIs, changes, and incidents, so evidence comes from live data
It removes the need to license separate IRM applications because ITSM licensing already covers them
It automatically marks every CI as compliant with ISO 27001 once the CMDB is populated and healthy
It lets IT staff approve and publish policies directly, without needing involvement from compliance
questions.explanation:
When a control about unapproved changes can query the change table directly, or a risk is scoped to a business application CI, evidence is collected from the system of record rather than requested by email. That is the practical meaning of continuous monitoring.

IRM applications are still licensed. Governance roles do not collapse into IT. No data model makes anything compliant automatically.

questions.stem: Which set of applications is generally considered the core of ServiceNow Integrated Risk Management?
options: Vendor Risk Management, Security Incident Response, and HR Service Delivery
Policy and Compliance Management, Risk Management, and Audit Management
Performance Analytics, Reporting, and Dashboards
Incident Management, Problem Management, and Change Management
questions.explanation:
Policy and Compliance, Risk, and Audit are the foundational IRM applications that CIS-RC centers on. Others — third-party risk, BCM, privacy, operational resilience — extend the same data model.

ITSM processes and reporting tools integrate with IRM but are not part of it. Vendor risk and security incident response are adjacent applications.

questions.stem: What is a control in ServiceNow Policy and Compliance?
options: A record that describes an external regulation, standard, or framework the organization must follow
A policy statement applied to one specific entity, which is then attested to, tested, and monitored
A permission that determines which users can read or edit risk and compliance records on the platform
A scheduled job that recalculates compliance scores for every policy and authority document nightly
questions.explanation:
A policy statement defines the objective. A control is that objective applied to one entity, and it is the record that gets attested, tested, and monitored by indicators. Its status rolls up into compliance scores.

External regulations are authority documents. Access is governed by roles and ACLs. Score calculation is a platform mechanism, not a control.

questions.stem: A company wants to implement Policy and Compliance and Risk Management across 40 business units and 12 regulations. What is the recommended approach?
options: Build custom tables for each business unit first, then migrate to the base data model in a later phase
Load every regulation and business unit in the first release so the data model is complete from day one
Start with a focused, high-value use case and a limited set of entities, prove value, then expand in phases
Implement Audit Management before anything else because it has the fewest dependencies on other data
questions.explanation:
Phased delivery starting from a narrow, meaningful scope is the consistent guidance: get the entity model, ownership, and attestation cycle working for one framework, then scale. Big-bang loads generate thousands of controls before owners are ready to act on them.

Customizing before adopting the base model creates technical debt. Audit is typically more valuable once controls exist to test.

questions.stem: Which persona is typically responsible for responding to control attestations?
options: The compliance manager in the second line
The internal auditor in the third line
The control owner in the first line
The GRC platform administrator
questions.explanation:
Control owners — first-line business users — attest whether their control is designed and operating. Compliance managers define the program and review results; auditors test independently; administrators configure the platform.

Expect persona questions that test which line of defense performs which activity.

questions.stem: Before configuring entity types, what information is most important to gather during planning?
options: Which tables hold the in-scope business units, applications, and vendors, and whether that data is accurate
The exact number of fulfiller and business-user licenses purchased for each IRM application
The branding, color scheme, and layout preferences for the risk and compliance workspaces
The full list of reports and dashboards that executives expect to see at the end of the first phase
questions.explanation:
Entity types are built on existing platform tables, so scoping depends on knowing where business units, applications, and other in-scope items live and whether the records are trustworthy. Poor source data produces entities with no owners and controls nobody can attest to.

Reporting needs matter later. Licensing and theming do not shape the entity model.

questions.stem: What is an entity in ServiceNow IRM?
options: A regulation or framework imported from a content provider and broken down into citations
Any record that risk and compliance work can be scoped to, such as a business unit, application, or vendor
A user who holds a GRC role and is responsible for attesting to controls or assessing risks
A configuration item in the CMDB; other tables cannot represent things in scope for compliance
questions.explanation:
Entities are the things you manage risk and compliance for. They can come from any table — CMDB classes, departments, companies, locations — which is why the framework works across use cases. Older releases called them profiles.

Users hold roles, regulations are authority documents, and limiting entities to the CMDB is a common wrong assumption.

questions.stem: Every business application with a criticality of "1 - most critical" must automatically come into scope for risk and compliance. What should you configure?
options: A policy exception that excludes every business application not rated 1 - most critical from scope
A scheduled script that copies critical business applications into a dedicated GRC table each night
An entity type on the business application table with the condition criticality = 1 - most critical
An entity class named "Critical" that business application owners assign to their applications
questions.explanation:
Entity types define a source table and a condition. Every record that matches becomes an entity, and new matches are picked up automatically, so scope tracks the source data without manual upkeep.

Copying records duplicates data. Entity classes group types rather than select records. Policy exceptions handle deviations from policy, not scoping.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an entity class?
options: It stores the attestation schedule and reminders used for controls on those entities
It sets a default inherent risk score that applies to every entity in that class
It groups entity types into broader categories, such as IT or Organization, for reporting
It defines which source table and filter condition the entities are generated from
questions.explanation:
Entity classes are a categorization layer above entity types — useful for reporting and for organizing a large entity model. The source table and condition live on the entity type.

Classes carry no scores or schedules.

questions.stem: A new business application is created that matches an existing entity type's condition. That entity type is in scope for two policy statements. What happens?
options: Nothing happens until an administrator manually runs an entity refresh for that entity type
Both policy statements are duplicated so the new application has its own copies to attest against
An entity is created automatically, and controls are generated for it from both policy statements
An entity is created automatically, but its controls must be added by the compliance manager by hand
questions.explanation:
Entity generation and control generation are both condition-driven: matching records become entities, and policy statements associated with that entity type generate one control per entity. That automation is what keeps scope current.

Policy statements are shared across entities, not duplicated. Manual control creation defeats the purpose of the framework.

questions.stem: A business application is retired and no longer meets its entity type's condition. What is the expected behavior?
options: The entity stays active, with its controls still in force, until an auditor formally closes it
The application is added back to scope automatically because entities cannot leave once created
The entity is deactivated and its controls and risks are retired, preserving their history
The entity and all of its controls and risks are permanently deleted to keep reporting accurate
questions.explanation:
When a source record falls out of scope, the entity is made inactive and the records generated from it are retired rather than deleted, so the compliance and risk history stays available for audit.

Deleting evidence would break audit trails. Leaving it active would misstate current scope.

questions.stem: Leadership wants compliance and risk to roll up from applications to the business units that own them. What enables this?
options: Making business units an entity class so the platform infers which applications belong to them
Adding the owning business unit's name into the description field of every generated control
Entity relationships that place each application below its owning business unit in a hierarchy
Writing a separate policy for each business unit so its controls can be reported on separately
questions.explanation:
Upstream and downstream entity relationships form the hierarchy that scores and reporting roll up through. Without them, every entity is an island.

Descriptions are not structured data. Separate policies fragment the program. A class label does not create parent-child relationships.

questions.stem: Why is it a poor idea to create an entity type that makes every CI in the CMDB an entity?
options: Configuration items cannot be assigned owners, so no one could attest to the generated controls
It creates huge numbers of unowned entities, controls, and risks, adding noise without improving assurance
Turning every CI into an entity disables the CMDB Health dashboard for the classes involved
Entity types are not permitted to reference CMDB tables, so the configuration would fail to save
questions.explanation:
Scope should reflect what is material. Each entity multiplies controls and risks across every associated statement, so indiscriminate scoping creates unmanageable workloads and dilutes attention on what matters.

CMDB tables are valid sources, and CIs can have owners. The CMDB dashboard is unaffected.

questions.stem: How does an entity end up with controls?
options: A compliance manager adds each relevant control to the entity by hand from the control library
The entity owner chooses which controls apply from a catalog during an annual scoping review
Controls are copied onto the entity directly from the authority documents that are in scope
Its entity type is associated with policy statements, and one control is generated per statement
questions.explanation:
Policy statements are scoped to entity types; the platform generates one control per entity per statement. That relationship is the core of the compliance data model.

Authority documents connect through citations to policy statements, not directly to entities. Owners attest to controls rather than choosing them.

questions.stem: Which tables can an entity type use as its source?
options: Only the department and company tables
Only tables in the CMDB
Only tables inside the GRC scoped applications
Any table on the platform
questions.explanation:
Any table can back an entity type — CMDB classes, core tables such as department, location, and company, or custom tables. That flexibility is why the framework supports such different use cases.

Restricting sources to the CMDB or to GRC tables is a common distractor.

questions.stem: Where does an entity's owner usually come from?
options: From the owner listed on the authority document that the entity's controls are mapped to
It is assigned round-robin to members of the GRC group when the entity is first generated
It is always the compliance manager who created the entity type, regardless of the source data
From an owner field on the source record that the entity type maps, such as the application owner
questions.explanation:
Entity types can map an owner field from the source table, so ownership follows the source data. That owner often becomes the default owner for generated controls and risks, which is why accurate ownership data matters in planning.

Owners do not come from authority documents, and assigning everything to the compliance manager breaks first-line accountability.

questions.stem: An implementer needs to confirm the table that stores entities. Which table is it?
options: sn_risk_risk
sn_compliance_control
cmdb_ci
sn_grc_profile
questions.explanation:
Entities kept their original "profile" table names when the feature was renamed, so entities are stored in sn_grc_profile, entity types in sn_grc_profile_type, and entity classes in sn_grc_profile_class.

Controls and risks have their own tables. cmdb_ci is a possible source table, not where entities live.

questions.stem: Select two benefits of building scope from entity types rather than adding entities manually. (Choose two.)
options: Ownership and attributes stay in sync with the system of record
Scope updates automatically as source records start or stop matching the condition
Entity types remove the need for policy statements
Entity types prevent controls from failing
questions.explanation:
Condition-driven entity types keep scope and ownership aligned with the source data without manual maintenance — new applications come into scope and retired ones fall out.

Policy statements are still what generate controls, and nothing about scoping prevents controls from failing.

questions.stem: A policy statement is associated with an entity type that has 25 entities. Three such statements apply. How many controls are generated?
questions.explanation:
One control is generated per entity for each policy statement: 25 entities × 3 statements = 75 controls.

This arithmetic shows why scoping discipline matters — controls multiply quickly.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between an authority document and a citation?
options: They are two names for the same record, used differently by compliance and audit teams
A citation is an internal policy, and the authority document is the record of its approval
Citations are attestation responses that control owners submit against an authority document
An authority document is an external regulation or standard; citations are its individual requirements
questions.explanation:
Authority documents represent regulations and frameworks such as ISO 27001 or HIPAA. Citations break them into individual requirements, which are mapped to internal policy statements to show how the organization meets each one.

Internal policies are separate records. Attestations are responses on controls.

questions.stem: How does an authority document's compliance status reflect the organization's actual controls?
options: It is calculated from the number of issues closed against the authority document's citations
Its citations map to policy statements, whose controls' statuses roll up into its compliance
The compliance manager enters it manually each quarter after reviewing control owner feedback
It is downloaded periodically from the content provider that supplied the authority document
questions.explanation:
The mapping chain is authority document → citations → policy statements → controls. Control results flow back up that chain, so compliance with a regulation reflects how the mapped controls are actually performing.

Manual entry and provider data would not reflect your environment. Closed issues are an input to remediation reporting, not the compliance calculation.

questions.stem: A control owner answers a control attestation indicating the control is not implemented. What is the expected outcome?
options: The entity is removed from scope until the control owner reports it is implemented
The underlying policy statement is retired because one of its controls has failed
The attestation is rejected as invalid and automatically resent to the control owner
The control becomes non-compliant, and an issue can be created to track remediation
questions.explanation:
Attestation responses set control status. A negative response marks the control non-compliant and, as typically configured, raises an issue so remediation is tracked.

The response is valid evidence — rejecting it would hide the gap. The policy statement and entity scope are unaffected by a single control result.

questions.stem: Which indicator type checks a condition against a table on the platform without requiring a script?
options: Basic indicator
Performance Analytics indicator
Script indicator
Manual indicator
questions.explanation:
Basic indicators evaluate a condition on a table — for example, whether any changes were implemented without approval. Manual indicators require a person to enter results; script indicators run custom logic; PA indicators use Performance Analytics data.

Prefer basic indicators where a condition is enough — they are easier to maintain.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a control attestation and a control test?
options: There is no meaningful difference; the platform uses the two terms interchangeably for the same record
An attestation is the owner's self-assessment; a control test is an independent check of effectiveness
Attestations apply only to IT general controls, while control tests apply to business process controls
Attestations are performed by internal auditors, while control tests are performed by control owners
questions.explanation:
Attestation is first-line self-assessment. Control testing is performed by the second or third line to validate that the control is designed properly and operating as intended.

Saying auditors attest and owners test inverts the roles. Attestations apply to any kind of control.

questions.stem: A business unit cannot comply with a policy statement for six months while a system is replaced. What should it request?
options: A time-bound policy exception with justification and approval, covering the affected controls
Deletion of the affected controls so they no longer count against the business unit's compliance
Retirement of the policy statement until the replacement system is fully in place
A new entity type whose condition excludes the business unit until the system is replaced
questions.explanation:
Policy exceptions formally record an approved, time-bound deviation for specific controls, often with compensating measures. The exception expires, so the gap cannot quietly become permanent.

Retiring the statement or deleting controls affects everyone and destroys history. Rewriting scope to dodge a requirement misrepresents compliance.

questions.stem: Policies need to be made available for employees to read and acknowledge. What capability supports this?
options: Emailing PDF copies from the compliance manager's mailbox and tracking replies manually
Creating a citation for each employee and mapping it to the relevant policy statements
Publishing the policy to a knowledge base and running a policy acknowledgment campaign
Adding every employee as a control owner so they attest to having read the policy
questions.explanation:
Published policies can be surfaced through the knowledge base, and acknowledgment campaigns ask users to confirm they have read them, producing evidence for auditors.

Email gives no tracked evidence. Making employees control owners or citations misuses those records.

questions.stem: Select two events that can make a control non-compliant. (Choose two.)
options: The entity owner's manager changes
The policy statement's category is edited
The control owner responds to an attestation that the control is not in place
An indicator associated with the control fails
questions.explanation:
Attestation responses and indicator results both feed control status. Either can surface a gap.

Organizational changes to the owner's manager and edits to categorization are administrative and do not evaluate the control.

questions.stem: Which state must a policy reach before it is considered in force and available to the organization?
options: In review
Retired
Draft
Published
questions.explanation:
Policies move through a lifecycle from draft, through review and approval, to published. Publishing is the point where the policy is in force; retired policies are no longer in effect.

Draft and review are working states.

questions.stem: How should evidence that a control is operating be provided during an attestation?
options: Attached to the attestation response or control record, so it stays with the result
Evidence is not needed, because attestations are self-assessments by the control owner
Saved in a shared drive folder, with the folder path pasted into a comment on the control
Emailed to the compliance manager, who files it in a shared mailbox for the auditors
questions.explanation:
Evidence belongs on the record it supports so reviewers and auditors can see it in context. Email and shared drives break the audit trail.

Self-assessments without evidence carry little assurance weight, which is why many programs require it.

questions.stem: An issue has been raised for a non-compliant control. Which outcomes can close it?
options: Issues close automatically after 30 days if no further activity is recorded on them
Only remediation; issues cannot be closed until the underlying gap has been fixed
Remediation, or a formal risk acceptance approved by the appropriate authority
Only deletion by the compliance manager once the business has reviewed the gap
questions.explanation:
Issues are resolved either by remediating the gap or by formally accepting the risk with appropriate approval. Both leave a record of the decision.

Deletion removes evidence, and nothing should close on a timer.

questions.stem: A policy statement is retired. What happens to the controls generated from it?
options: They are reassigned to another policy statement
They are deleted
They remain active and must be retired individually
They are retired, preserving their history
questions.explanation:
Retirement cascades to generated controls so they stop being attested and monitored, while their history remains for audit.

Deleting them would destroy evidence. Leaving them active would generate work against a statement that no longer applies.

questions.stem: Which table stores controls in Policy and Compliance Management?
options: sn_compliance_policy_statement
sn_compliance_policy
sn_compliance_control
sn_grc_profile_type
questions.explanation:
Controls live in sn_compliance_control, policies in sn_compliance_policy, and policy statements in sn_compliance_policy_statement. Entity types are sn_grc_profile_type.

Know the core tables — they appear in configuration and reporting questions.

questions.stem: What does a policy statement represent?
options: A control objective the organization commits to, which generates controls for in-scope entities
An employee's recorded acknowledgment that they have read and understood a published policy
A specific control as implemented on one entity, with its own owner and attestation history
A single section or requirement of an external regulation, imported from a content provider
questions.explanation:
Policy statements are the requirements inside a policy. Applied to entity types, they generate controls. Mapping them to citations links internal requirements to external regulations.

Per-entity implementations are controls. Regulation sections are citations. Acknowledgments are campaign responses.

questions.stem: What is a risk statement?
options: A reusable risk definition in the library that generates risks for in-scope entities
A formal approval recording that a risk owner has accepted a risk above appetite
An executive summary of the organization's risk posture, prepared for the board each quarter
A risk recorded against one specific entity, with its own owner and assessment history
questions.explanation:
Risk statements are library entries — "unauthorized access to sensitive data" — that, when associated with entity types, generate a risk record for each entity. This mirrors how policy statements generate controls.

The per-entity record is the risk itself.

questions.stem: Which pairing of definitions is correct?
options: Inherent risk is exposure before controls are considered; residual risk is what remains after controls
Inherent and residual risk are always equal until a target risk assessment has been completed
Residual risk is the level the organization wants to reach once planned responses are in place
Inherent risk is exposure after controls are considered; residual risk is exposure before controls
questions.explanation:
Inherent risk ignores controls. Residual risk reflects the effect of existing controls. Target risk is the desired level after planned responses.

Swapping "before" and "after" controls inverts the definitions; target risk is a separate assessment.

questions.stem: In advanced risk assessment, what does a risk assessment methodology define?
options: The assessment types, factors, and scoring used to assess risks consistently
The authority documents and citations that each risk statement is mapped to
The entity hierarchy that risks roll up through for business unit reporting
Which users and groups can view, edit, and approve risk records within each entity
questions.explanation:
A methodology defines how risk is measured: which assessments are performed (such as inherent, control, residual, target), which factors are asked, and how answers become scores. Consistency across assessments depends on it.

Access, hierarchy, and regulatory mapping are configured elsewhere.

questions.stem: A risk team wants to estimate annual loss in currency using single loss expectancy and annual rate of occurrence. Which approach fits?
options: An entity class that groups the affected entities by their potential financial loss
Quantitative factors that calculate annualized loss expectancy as SLE × ARO
Qualitative factors that rate likelihood and impact on a high, medium, and low scale
A policy exception that records the expected loss and its approved duration
questions.explanation:
Quantitative assessment produces monetary values; ALE = SLE × ARO is the classic formula. Qualitative factors are rating scales and do not produce currency estimates.

Exceptions and entity classes are unrelated to scoring.

questions.stem: An organization buys cyber insurance to cover the financial impact of a data breach. Which risk response is this?
options: Avoid
Mitigate
Accept
Transfer
questions.explanation: Insurance shifts financial consequences to a third party — risk transfer. Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact through controls, avoidance stops the activity, and acceptance takes the risk as is.

questions.stem: What should a well-run program require when a risk is accepted?
options: Automatic transfer of the risk to internal audit for independent review and sign-off
Nothing further; accepting a risk simply closes it and removes it from future assessments
Approval by an appropriate authority, a documented rationale, and an expiration date
Deletion of the related controls, since they no longer need to be attested to
questions.explanation:
Acceptance is a decision someone must own. Approval, rationale, and an expiry ensure the decision is revisited as conditions change.

Accepting a risk does not close it permanently, remove controls, or hand it to audit.

questions.stem: What is the role of key risk indicators associated with a risk?
options: They replace periodic risk assessments once enough indicator history has been collected
They store the approvals and rationale recorded when a risk owner accepts the risk
They set the inherent risk score directly from the most recent indicator result
They track measurable signals tied to the risk and flag threshold breaches between assessments
questions.explanation:
KRIs provide continuous signal — for example, the count of critical vulnerabilities older than 30 days — and alert when thresholds are crossed. They complement periodic assessments.

They don't set scores or store approvals.

questions.stem: How is residual risk typically derived in an advanced risk assessment?
options: It is copied from the target risk assessment once remediation has been planned
From inherent risk, adjusted by the assessed effectiveness of the related controls
By averaging all of the risk's historical assessment scores over the past year
From the number of open issues currently linked to the risk and its entity
questions.explanation:
Residual risk combines the inherent assessment with a control effectiveness assessment. Strong controls reduce residual exposure; weak ones leave it near inherent.

Issue counts and target values are inputs to other decisions, not the residual calculation.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of recording risk events?
options: To capture actual losses and near misses, link them to risks, and inform assessments
To create new entities automatically for business units affected by an incident
To record approvals when a risk owner accepts a risk that exceeds appetite
To schedule audit engagements for entities that have experienced repeated losses
questions.explanation:
Risk events document what actually happened — losses, near misses — and link back to related risks. That history improves estimates, especially in quantitative models.

Approvals, audit scheduling, and entity creation are unrelated.

questions.stem: What does a risk heat map typically plot?
options: Users against roles
Number of controls against number of entities
Likelihood against impact
Audit findings against issue age
questions.explanation: Heat maps place risks on a likelihood-versus-impact grid so the most significant risks stand out. The other pairings are not standard risk visualizations.

questions.stem: A risk manager wants to compare a risk's residual score against how much risk the organization is willing to take. What concept applies?
options: Citation
Risk appetite
Inherent risk
Entity class
questions.explanation:
Risk appetite expresses the level of risk the organization is willing to accept. Residual risk above appetite should drive a response.

Inherent risk is pre-control exposure. Entity classes and citations are structural records.

questions.stem: Ten applications are entities of a type associated with one risk statement. How many risks are generated?
options: None until each is created manually
questions.explanation: One risk per entity per associated risk statement: 10 entities × 1 statement = 10 risks. Generation is automatic, just as with controls.

questions.stem: Select two sources that commonly inform risk identification. (Choose two.)
options: Recorded risk events and incidents
The entity class label
Deleted CI records
The risk statement library
questions.explanation:
Library statements provide standard risk definitions, and actual events reveal risks the library may have missed or underweighted.

A class label provides no risk information, and deleted records are not a meaningful input.

questions.stem: Leadership wants a single view of risk for each business unit, including risks on applications the unit owns. What makes this possible?
options: A separate risk framework per business unit
Making every application a business unit
Exporting every risk to a spreadsheet
Risk aggregation through the entity hierarchy
questions.explanation:
Because risks belong to entities and entities sit in a hierarchy, risk can roll up from applications to their business units. That is the payoff of modeling entity relationships.

Spreadsheets lose the live connection. Restructuring entities or frameworks to fake a roll-up creates more problems than it solves.

questions.stem: What does a target risk assessment represent?
options: The risk level the organization aims to reach after planned responses are in place
The level of risk exposure before any controls or responses are taken into account
The risk level reported by external auditors at the end of their annual engagement
The highest score the risk assessment methodology can produce for any single risk
questions.explanation:
Target risk is the desired end state. The gap between residual and target justifies planned remediation work.

Pre-control risk is inherent. External audit opinions and maximum scores are different concepts.

questions.stem: A compliance team wants to load ISO, NIST, and other frameworks with their requirements already mapped to common controls. Which integration supports this?
options: Unified Compliance Framework (UCF) content import
IntegrationHub spoke for Slack
Service Graph Connector for Microsoft SCCM
Discovery
questions.explanation:
The UCF integration imports authority documents, citations, and common controls with their cross-mappings, which accelerates test-once-comply-many programs.

Slack, Discovery, and SCCM integrations serve different purposes.

questions.stem: What does regulatory change management add to a risk and compliance program?
options: It replaces policy exceptions with regulator-approved waivers for affected business units
It tracks regulatory changes, assesses their impact on policies and controls, and drives updates
It schedules control attestations to coincide with the effective dates of new regulations
It automatically deletes authority documents that a regulator has replaced or withdrawn
questions.explanation:
Regulatory change management takes in notices of new or changed regulations, assesses which parts of your program they affect, and drives tasks to update policies and controls.

It doesn't delete documents, replace exceptions, or schedule attestations.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of continuous monitoring using data from another ServiceNow application?
options: An indicator that queries change requests for changes implemented without approval
An audit engagement scheduled every three years to test change management controls
An annual attestation emailed to each control owner with a reminder before the due date
A quarterly spreadsheet review of change logs exported from the change management tool
questions.explanation: Continuous monitoring uses indicators against live platform data — here, change records — to detect control failures as they occur. Annual attestations and triennial audits are periodic.

questions.stem: Why do Policy and Compliance, Risk, and Audit share a common issue record?
options: So remediation is tracked consistently and findings from any source appear in one place
To prevent issues from being assigned to owners outside the application that created them
They don't; each application keeps a separate issue table that must be reconciled manually
Because issues can only be created by auditors, who need to share them with other teams
questions.explanation:
A shared issue model means a failed control, an assessed risk, or an audit observation all produce the same kind of remediation record with owners and due dates. Reporting on open findings spans the program.

Issues can come from any source and must be assigned to be worked.

questions.stem: Select two ways IRM extends its value through common platform capabilities. (Choose two.)
options: Using reporting and dashboards to show compliance and risk posture
Using workflow and notifications to route attestations, approvals, and remediation
Storing evidence outside the platform by default
Bypassing role-based access control for GRC data
questions.explanation:
IRM uses standard platform workflow, notifications, reporting, and dashboards, so it behaves like the rest of the platform and is easy to extend.

Bypassing access control or moving evidence off-platform would weaken the program.

questions.stem: What is an audit engagement?
options: A planned audit, scoped to entities, that organizes activities, testing, and observations
A policy acknowledgment campaign that internal audit runs for employees each year
A formal risk acceptance reviewed and approved by the chief audit executive
A single control attestation that an auditor sends to a control owner for completion
questions.explanation:
Engagements are the container for an audit: scope (entities), plan, activities, control tests, and findings. They move through their own lifecycle.

Attestations, acceptances, and acknowledgments belong to other processes.

questions.stem: During fieldwork, an auditor notes a potential weakness. How does this typically progress?
options: It is recorded as an observation and, if confirmed, an issue is raised for remediation
It is recorded directly as a policy exception against the affected policy statement
It is added as a new citation on the authority document the weakness relates to
It is discussed verbally with management and not recorded until the final report
questions.explanation:
Observations capture findings during the engagement. Confirmed findings become issues with owners and remediation plans, using the same issue model as the rest of IRM.

Exceptions and citations serve different purposes, and unrecorded findings provide no assurance.

questions.stem: What is a key benefit of running Audit Management on the same data as Policy and Compliance?
options: Auditors can test controls the business already defined and attested, instead of a separate set
Auditors no longer need to remain independent, since they share data with the first line
Controls that have been attested by their owners no longer need any independent testing
Audit engagements replace control attestations, so control owners no longer need to respond
questions.explanation:
Shared controls let the third line test what the first and second lines rely on, which reduces duplication and makes findings directly actionable.

Independence still matters, attestations still have a role, and controls still need testing.

questions.stem: Business units complain that risk, compliance, and audit teams each ask them for the same evidence. How does an integrated program address this?
options: Evidence and control results live on shared records that all three functions use
Each team keeps its own evidence repository so requests can be tracked separately
Audit takes over all evidence collection on behalf of risk and compliance
Business units stop providing evidence and teams rely on interviews instead
questions.explanation:
"Audit fatigue" comes from disconnected programs asking the same questions. When controls, evidence, and results sit on shared records, each function reuses what already exists instead of re-requesting it.

Separate repositories are the cause, not the cure. Interviews alone provide weak assurance, and centralizing everything in audit compromises its independence.

questions.stem: Which executive most commonly sponsors an enterprise risk management program?
options: The chief risk officer
The head of facilities
The service desk manager
The chief marketing officer
questions.explanation:
The CRO typically owns the enterprise risk framework and is the natural sponsor for risk management on the platform, alongside the chief compliance officer and chief audit executive for their areas.

The other roles are stakeholders at most.

questions.stem: In GRC, what does "governance" refer to?
options: The process of testing controls to confirm they operate effectively over time
The technical controls that block unauthorized access to networks and systems
How leadership sets direction, assigns accountability, and oversees the business
The regulatory filings and reports submitted to government agencies each year
questions.explanation:
Governance is direction and oversight — strategy, policies, roles, and accountability set by leadership and the board. Risk management and compliance operate within it.

Technical controls, testing, and filings are activities inside the program, not governance itself.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between compliance management and risk management?
options: Compliance covers meeting obligations; risk covers uncertainty affecting objectives
They are identical disciplines that different industries simply name differently
Compliance is optional for most companies, while risk management is legally required
Compliance is performed only by internal audit, and risk management only by IT
questions.explanation:
Compliance asks "are we meeting our obligations?" Risk asks "what could prevent us from achieving our objectives, and how much exposure do we accept?" They overlap — non-compliance is itself a risk — but they are distinct.

Neither belongs to a single team, and neither is universally optional.

questions.stem: What is a common controls framework?
options: A framework of controls that applies only to financial reporting under SOX
One set of internal controls mapped to the overlapping requirements of many regulations
A ServiceNow plugin that generates new controls automatically from resolved incidents
A separate list of controls kept for each regulation so their requirements never mix
questions.explanation:
A common controls framework rationalizes overlapping requirements into one internal control set, mapped to each regulation. It's the structure behind test-once-comply-many.

Keeping separate control lists per regulation is the problem it solves.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of continuous monitoring over periodic control assessments?
options: It shortens the time between a control failing and someone noticing
It removes the need to map controls to regulations and authority documents
It guarantees that controls never fail between scheduled assessments
It removes the need for control owners because monitoring runs on its own
questions.explanation:
Periodic assessments can leave a failure undetected for months. Continuous monitoring evaluates data on a schedule and surfaces failures soon after they happen.

Owners still remediate, controls still fail, and regulatory mapping still matters.

questions.stem: What is a risk register?
options: A list of every user who holds the risk manager or risk admin role
A register of external regulations and standards the company follows
A log of every configuration change made to the risk application
A catalog of identified risks with their owners, ratings, and responses
questions.explanation:
The risk register is the inventory of risks the organization is managing — who owns them, how they're rated, and what's being done. In ServiceNow, risk records against entities form it.

User lists, audit logs, and regulation lists are separate things.

questions.stem: Why do organizations use control self-assessment?
options: To have the people operating controls evaluate them and surface gaps early
To let control owners approve their own policy exceptions without review
To replace independent internal audit entirely with first-line reviews
To avoid the effort of documenting controls in a formal control library
questions.explanation:
Self-assessment puts first-line owners in the habit of checking their own controls, which surfaces problems earlier and cheaper than waiting for audit.

It complements independent assurance rather than replacing it, and it doesn't extend to approving exceptions.

questions.stem: What is a key control?
options: A control whose failure would leave a significant risk unaddressed
Any control that relies on encryption keys or key management systems
The first control created when a new policy statement is published
A control owned by a member of the executive leadership team
questions.explanation:
Key controls are the ones the organization relies on most to address significant risks or requirements. They typically receive more frequent testing and closer scrutiny.

The term has nothing to do with encryption, seniority of the owner, or creation order.

questions.stem: Why automate control evidence collection where possible?
options: Automatically collected evidence never needs to be reviewed by anyone
It removes the need for control owners once collection is automated
It cuts manual effort and yields more consistent, timely evidence
Regulators accept only automated evidence for technology controls
questions.explanation:
Automated evidence — from indicators querying platform data — is consistent, timely, and cheap to collect repeatedly.

It still needs review, regulators accept many forms of evidence, and owners still own the control.

questions.stem: Which is a characteristic of a mature integrated risk management program?
options: Compliance and risk teams use separate tools that never share data
Decisions draw on current, shared risk data from across the business
Issues are tracked in email threads until audit asks to see them
Each department assesses risk once a year in its own spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Maturity means risk is part of decision-making and based on current, integrated data. The other options describe the siloed, periodic programs that IRM replaces.

questions.stem: During implementation, who is typically responsible for configuring entity types, policy settings, and assessment templates?
options: Any user who has read access to risk and compliance records
The external auditors who will review the program each year
Each control owner, for the controls assigned to them
A GRC administrator or implementer with the right admin role
questions.explanation:
Program configuration belongs to administrators with GRC admin roles, working with compliance and risk managers to reflect agreed design.

Control owners attest; auditors stay independent; read-only users can't configure anything.

questions.stem: What is the recommended approach when existing processes don't match the base application?
options: Replace the base tables with custom ones built from scratch
Customize the application heavily to mirror every existing process step
Delay the implementation until the base application matches current processes
Document current processes, adopt base functionality where possible, and justify deviations
questions.explanation:
Adopting base functionality keeps upgrades simple and gets value sooner. Customize only where there's a clear, justified need.

Heavy customization creates technical debt, waiting gains nothing, and replacing base tables abandons the platform's capabilities.

questions.stem: Why should success measures be defined early in an IRM implementation?
options: They replace the need for a project plan, since they describe what will be delivered
They determine how many fulfiller and business-user licenses need to be purchased
They let the team show value, such as on-time attestations or fewer audit findings
They are a technical prerequisite that must be met before the plugins can be activated
questions.explanation:
Defining measures up front — attestation completion rates, time to remediate issues, audit findings — gives the program a way to prove value and steer.

They aren't technical prerequisites, plans, or licensing inputs.

questions.stem: Why involve control owners and business users early in the implementation?
options: Their adoption decides whether attestations and remediation happen
They must approve and sign the platform license agreement before go-live
They need to write the scripts and code that the application relies on
They are responsible for configuring the entity types and policy settings
questions.explanation:
IRM depends on first-line participation. Owners who understand why the program matters and how to use it respond to attestations and fix issues; owners who are surprised by it don't.

They don't code, sign licenses, or configure the platform.

questions.stem: An administrator narrows an entity type's condition so that fewer records match. What happens to entities whose records no longer match?
options: They are permanently deleted along with all of their compliance and risk history
They become inactive, and their generated controls and risks are retired
They remain active and keep their controls until someone removes them manually
They move automatically to whichever other entity type their records still match
questions.explanation:
Entity membership follows the condition. Records that no longer match fall out of scope, and the records generated from them are retired rather than deleted.

Entities don't move to other types on their own, and history is preserved.

questions.stem: Business units should be entities so policies can be assigned to them. Which table is a typical source?
options: The department or business unit table
The system log table for each department
The user preferences table for managers
The incident table, filtered by assignment group
questions.explanation:
Organizational tables such as department (cmn_department) or business unit are the natural sources for organizational entities.

Incidents, preferences, and logs are transactional or system data, not things you scope compliance to.

questions.stem: A company wants every active vendor to be an entity so it can assess third-party risk. What is a typical entity type configuration?
options: A manually maintained spreadsheet of vendors imported into a custom table
The company table, with a condition such as vendor = true and status = active
The user table, filtered to users whose email address uses a vendor's domain
The incident table, filtered to incidents that were raised by vendor contacts
questions.explanation:
Vendors are usually companies flagged as vendors, so the company table with a vendor condition generates vendor entities automatically.

Users and incidents don't represent vendors, and spreadsheets lose automation.

questions.stem: An application's owner changes in the CMDB. Why does it matter that the entity type maps its owner field from the source record?
options: It prevents the application's owner from ever being changed in the CMDB
The entity owner stays in sync with the system of record automatically
It forces a new risk assessment every time the application owner changes
It deletes the previous owner's user record once the new owner is set
questions.explanation:
Mapping ownership from the source keeps the entity's owner current as the source changes, so attestations and tasks route to the right person.

Mapping doesn't freeze ownership, delete users, or trigger assessments.

questions.stem: In an entity hierarchy, what does "upstream" mean?
options: The parent entity others roll up to, such as a business unit above its apps
An entity that is owned and managed by an external third party
The entity that was created most recently within the same entity type
An entity that currently has one or more failing or non-compliant controls
questions.explanation:
Upstream entities sit above others in the hierarchy; downstream entities sit below and roll up into them.

The terms describe position in the hierarchy, not age, ownership, or status.

questions.stem: How can relationships between entities be created automatically from existing data?
options: With entity type relationships based on reference fields between source tables
By creating each relationship by hand on the entity form, one entity at a time
They can't be automated; relationships must be maintained in a separate spreadsheet
By importing the relationships from the authority document's citation hierarchy
questions.explanation:
Entity type relationships can use references between source records — such as an application's owning department — to build the entity hierarchy automatically.

Manual relationships don't scale, and authority documents contain no organizational structure.

questions.stem: Which statement about a single entity is true?
options: It can be used only by Policy and Compliance, not by Risk or Audit
It can have controls or risks associated with it, but never both together
It must be duplicated so each IRM application has its own copy to use
It can have controls, risks, and audit scope associated with it at once
questions.explanation:
Entities are shared across IRM applications. The same application entity can have controls, risks, indicators, and be in audit scope — which is what makes integrated reporting possible.

Duplicating entities per application would recreate silos.

questions.stem: A policy statement should apply only to business applications that process payment data. Most business applications don't. What is a clean way to scope it?
options: Associate it with all business applications and have owners ignore extra controls
Create a narrower entity type for payment-processing applications and use it
Create the needed controls manually on each payment-processing application
Add the payment requirement to the description of every related policy statement
questions.explanation:
A narrower entity type, using a condition such as "processes cardholder data = true", generates controls only where the requirement applies.

Over-scoping creates noise, manual controls lose automation, and descriptions aren't scoping.

questions.stem: A server is both a production asset and part of the PCI environment, and two entity types match it. What is the expected behavior?
options: The server is excluded from both entity types
A single entity is associated with both entity types
The platform rejects the second entity type
Two duplicate entities are created for the same server
questions.explanation:
One record yields one entity, which can belong to several entity types. Each type contributes its own policy statements and risk statements, so there's no duplication.

Duplicates would split history, and overlapping types are normal.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an entity owner and a control owner?
options: The entity owner is accountable for the entity; a control owner operates one control
They are always the same person, and the platform won't allow them to differ
Entity owners are always auditors, while control owners are always risk managers
The control owner approves entity types, while the entity owner writes the policies
questions.explanation:
Ownership can be split: an application owner may own the entity while specific controls belong to the DBA team or security operations. Control owners often default from the entity owner, but they can be reassigned.

Neither role writes policies or audits.

questions.stem: How does the entity framework support audit planning?
options: Entities are hidden from audit users to preserve the independence of the third line
Auditors must create their own separate copy of each entity before planning begins
Engagements can be scoped to entities, bringing in their controls, risks, and issues
Audit planning uses only authority documents, so entities play no part in it
questions.explanation:
Scoping engagements by entity brings the related controls, risks, and issues into the audit, so auditors work from the same picture as the first and second lines.

Copies would break the integrated model.

questions.stem: Should a company use business applications or individual application services as entities for application controls?
options: Always application services, because there are more of them to assess
Neither, because applications aren't allowed to be used as entities
Whichever level matches where ownership sits and controls are operated
Always business applications, because they're stored in the CMDB
questions.explanation:
Choose the level where accountability and control operation sit. If controls differ between production and test, application services may be right. If one owner manages the whole application, the business application may be enough.

Counting records isn't a design principle, and both are valid sources.

questions.stem: Physical security controls must be attested for each office. What is a sensible entity source?
options: The user table, filtered to facilities staff
The change request table
The location table, filtered to office locations
The knowledge base
questions.explanation:
Locations represent offices, so a location-based entity type gives each office its own physical security controls.

Facilities staff are owners, not scope. Changes and articles aren't places.

questions.stem: Controls are being generated without owners. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The source records behind the entities have no value in the mapped owner field
The risk heat map hasn't been configured, which blocks owner assignment
The policy statements are still unpublished, so owners can't be assigned yet
The authority documents are missing citations, so ownership can't be derived
questions.explanation:
Owners flow from the source data through the entity. If the mapped owner field is empty on the source records, generated controls have no one to route to. Fix the source data or the mapping.

Policy state, citations, and heat maps don't affect ownership.

questions.stem: Where can a compliance manager see the controls, risks, issues, and indicators related to a single entity?
options: Nowhere; that information isn't connected
Only by exporting each table to a spreadsheet
On the entity record and its related views
Only in a custom report built for each entity
questions.explanation:
The entity is the hub of the data model, so its record and related views bring together everything scoped to it.

Custom reports and exports are possible but unnecessary for this.

questions.stem: A source record behind an entity is deleted. What should happen?
options: The entity is recreated automatically from the related authority document
Nothing happens; the entity stays active indefinitely without a source
The entity becomes inactive and its records are retired, keeping history
All related issues are closed automatically and marked as remediated
questions.explanation:
Without a source record, the entity is no longer in scope. Retiring rather than deleting keeps the history auditors need.

Entities don't come from authority documents, staying active misstates scope, and closing issues as remediated would be false.

questions.stem: Only applications that are in production should be in scope for an application entity type. How should this be handled?
options: Ask application owners to decline attestations for non-production applications
Include an operational status condition in the entity type so only production applications match
Create a separate policy for non-production applications that has no statements
Create entities for all applications and retire non-production ones by hand each month
questions.explanation:
Conditions on the entity type keep scope accurate automatically as application status changes.

Manual cleanup, declined attestations, and empty policies are workarounds for a missing condition.

questions.stem: A compliance team wants Linux servers and Oracle databases in scope for the same hardening policy. How many source tables can a single entity type use?
options: One, so use an entity type per table or one on a shared parent class with a condition
None, because entity types reference entity classes rather than tables directly
Any number of tables, listed together in the entity type's source table field
Two at most, one primary table and one secondary table for related records
questions.explanation:
An entity type points at one table. To cover servers and databases, create one entity type for each, or use a common parent class such as cmdb_ci with a condition that selects both. Either way, the policy statement can be associated with each type.

Entity types reference tables, not classes, and there's no multi-table field.

questions.stem: How do policies, standards, and procedures typically relate in a policy framework?
options: Policies state intent, standards set specific requirements, procedures give steps
Standards are optional guidance that teams can choose whether or not to follow
They are three names for the same document, used interchangeably by different teams
Procedures are the highest level, and policies hold the most detailed instructions
questions.explanation:
Policies express what the organization commits to, standards make it specific and measurable, and procedures explain the steps. ServiceNow lets you model them so controls trace back to the right level.

Inverting the hierarchy or treating standards as optional misunderstands the framework.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for a policy's content and its periodic review?
options: The platform administrator
Every control owner
The policy owner
The external auditor
questions.explanation: Policy owners maintain the content and keep it current. Approvers sign off, control owners operate controls under it, and auditors evaluate it independently.

questions.stem: A policy should be reviewed every year to make sure it is still accurate. How is this best supported?
options: Set a review frequency or next review date on the policy to trigger a review
Republish the policy automatically every year so it is always marked as current
Delete the policy and recreate it from scratch every year with updated content
Ask the policy owner to remember to check the policy around the same time each year
questions.explanation:
Review dates and cadence fields make the review a tracked obligation instead of something people have to remember.

Automatic republishing skips the review, and recreating policies destroys history.

questions.stem: A published policy needs a substantive change. What is the appropriate way to handle it?
options: Retire the policy and stop tracking it, since the content is now out of date
Revise it through the lifecycle so the change is reviewed and approved first
Edit the published text directly so the change takes effect immediately for everyone
Email the change to employees and leave the published record as it is
questions.explanation:
Changes go back through review and approval so the published version always reflects something that was approved, and the history shows what changed.

Editing in place bypasses approval, retiring abandons the requirement, and email leaves the record wrong.

questions.stem: An authority document has sections, subsections, and individual requirements. How are these represented?
options: As separate authority documents for each subsection
As a hierarchy of citations under the authority document
As policy statements under the authority document
As attachments on the authority document record
questions.explanation:
Citations can be organized hierarchically to mirror the document's structure, and individual requirement citations are what get mapped to policy statements.

Splitting into many authority documents fragments reporting; policy statements are internal; attachments aren't mappable.

questions.stem: Which statement about mapping citations to policy statements is true?
options: Citations map to controls directly, so policy statements aren't involved in the mapping
Each policy statement can map to only one citation, from one authority document
Many-to-many: a statement can meet several citations, and a citation can need several statements
Each citation must map to exactly one policy statement, so coverage stays easy to trace
questions.explanation:
Regulations overlap and requirements can be broad, so mappings go both ways. That flexibility is what lets one internal requirement satisfy many regulations.

Citations connect to policy statements, which in turn generate controls.

questions.stem: A control requires a manager to approve user access requests before access is granted. What type of control is this?
options: Preventive
Corrective
Detective
Compensating
questions.explanation: Approval before access stops the problem from happening, which makes it preventive. Detective controls find issues after the fact, corrective controls fix them, and compensating controls stand in when a primary control can't be met.

questions.stem: A monthly review of firewall logs identifies unauthorized connection attempts. What type of control is this?
options: Deterrent
Directive
Preventive
Detective
questions.explanation: Reviewing logs to find events that already happened is detective. Preventive controls block events, directive controls instruct behavior (like policies), and deterrent controls discourage attempts.

questions.stem: Why are automated controls often preferred over manual ones where feasible?
options: Automated controls don't need an owner because the system operates them
Automated controls never fail once they have been configured correctly
Auditors don't accept manual controls as evidence for any regulation
They run consistently and can be monitored continuously with less effort
questions.explanation:
Automated controls run the same way every time and lend themselves to indicator-based monitoring.

They can still fail or be misconfigured, manual controls are accepted, and automated controls still need owners.

questions.stem: How is the frequency of control attestations typically managed?
options: Control owners attest whenever they happen to have time available
With an attestation schedule configured for the relevant controls
Attestations are sent to every control owner every single day
Attestations run only when an auditor specifically requests them
questions.explanation:
Scheduled attestations ensure controls are assessed at a defined cadence, such as quarterly or annually, depending on the control.

Ad hoc timing gives inconsistent coverage, waiting for auditors defeats self-assessment, and daily attestations create fatigue.

questions.stem: What platform capability is used to design the questions in a control attestation?
options: The assessment designer in the Survey and Assessment framework
Flow Designer subflows built for each policy statement
The service catalog item designer and its variable editor
The knowledge article editor used for published policies
questions.explanation: Attestations are assessments, so their questions are built with the assessment designer. Flows orchestrate processes, catalog items handle requests, and knowledge articles hold content.

questions.stem: Where are the outcomes of each indicator run recorded?
options: They aren't stored; only the latest pass or fail status is shown
As indicator result records linked to the indicator and its control
As attachments added to the related policy after each run completes
In the system log only, where administrators can search for them
questions.explanation:
Each run produces an indicator result, so you have a history of passes and failures over time — useful as evidence and for spotting trends.

Logs and attachments aren't the evidence model, and history is kept.

questions.stem: A team already tracks "percentage of servers patched within 30 days" as a Performance Analytics KPI. What is the simplest way to use it for a control?
options: A script indicator that recalculates the patching percentage from scratch
A Performance Analytics indicator using the existing KPI with a threshold
A manual indicator where someone types the KPI value in each month
An attestation asking the control owner to estimate the percentage
questions.explanation:
PA indicators reuse existing PA data and apply a threshold, so you don't rebuild the metric.

Rewriting the calculation duplicates work, and manual entry or estimates weaken evidence.

questions.stem: An indicator fails. What can a well-configured indicator do automatically?
options: Delete the related control from the entity
Create an issue for the related control
Approve a policy exception for the owner
Retire the parent policy statement
questions.explanation:
Indicators can be configured to raise issues on failure, turning a detected problem into tracked work.

Deleting controls, retiring statements, or approving exceptions are decisions for people, not automated outcomes of a failed check.

questions.stem: What is the difference between testing a control's design effectiveness and its operating effectiveness?
options: Operating effectiveness is tested only once, when the control is first created and approved
Design effectiveness is tested by control owners, while operating effectiveness is tested by vendors
Design asks if the control would work as described; operating asks if it actually ran that way over time
They are the same test performed twice, once by the first line and once by internal audit
questions.explanation:
A well-designed control can still fail in practice, and a control that runs every day can still be poorly designed. Testing both gives full assurance.

Who tests and how often depends on the program, not on these definitions.

questions.stem: How does a policy statement's compliance status relate to its controls?
options: It is copied from the compliance status of the mapped authority document
It has no relationship to its controls and is reported separately
It reflects the status of its generated controls across in-scope entities
It is set manually by the policy owner at the end of each quarter
questions.explanation:
Control results roll up to the policy statement, showing how well that requirement is met across the organization, and further up to policies and authority documents.

Manual entry and copying from authority documents wouldn't reflect reality.

questions.stem: A policy exception expires. What should happen to the affected controls?
options: They return to normal assessment, and any remaining gap shows as non-compliance
They remain exempt permanently, since the exception has already been approved once
The policy statement is retired automatically for every entity in scope
They are deleted, because the exception means they no longer need to be tracked
questions.explanation:
Exceptions are time-bound by design. When one expires, the controls are assessed normally again, so an unresolved gap becomes visible.

Permanent exemption or deletion would hide the gap, and the statement still applies to everyone else.

questions.stem: A system can't enforce multifactor authentication, so the team adds extra monitoring and quarterly access reviews instead. What are these additional measures called?
options: Citations
Compensating controls
Entity classes
Key risk indicators
questions.explanation:
Compensating controls reduce risk when a required control can't be implemented. They're often documented as part of a policy exception.

KRIs measure risk, citations are regulatory requirements, and entity classes are scoping categories.

questions.stem: A new security policy should be acknowledged only by employees in the engineering department. How should the campaign be set up?
options: Target the campaign to users who meet the engineering department criteria
Send the campaign to all employees and ask everyone else to ignore it
Create an entity for each engineer so the policy applies to them directly
Make each engineer a control owner for the policy so they attest to it
questions.explanation:
Acknowledgment campaigns can target an audience by criteria, so only the right people receive them and completion rates mean something.

Over-sending creates noise, and controls or entities aren't the mechanism for acknowledgment.

questions.stem: A control owner leaves the company. What is the best way to keep the control assigned correctly?
options: Delete the control now and recreate it once a replacement owner is hired
Mark the control compliant until a new owner has been found and assigned
Update ownership on the entity or control so attestations route to the new owner
Leave the control assigned to the former employee until an auditor notices
questions.explanation:
Reassigning ownership, ideally by correcting the source data that feeds entity ownership, keeps the control accountable without losing history.

Orphaned assignments, deleted controls, and false compliance all create audit findings.

questions.stem: A single citation requires both encryption at rest and encryption in transit, which are separate policy statements. How is this mapped?
options: Map only the more important statement, since one mapping is enough
Split the citation into two separate authority documents, one per statement
Map the citation to both statements, so its compliance depends on both
Create a new policy statement that copies the text of both existing ones
questions.explanation:
A citation can map to several statements when meeting it takes more than one internal requirement. Its compliance then reflects all of them.

Mapping one would overstate compliance, splitting authority documents breaks fidelity to the source, and duplicating statements creates redundant controls.

questions.stem: A control doesn't apply to a particular entity — for example, a database control on an application with no database. What is the right handling?
options: Mark it compliant so it doesn't lower the score
Delete the entity so the control disappears
Leave the attestation unanswered indefinitely
Record it as not applicable with a justification
questions.explanation:
A documented not-applicable decision is honest and auditable, and it shouldn't distort compliance scores. If it happens a lot, the entity type scoping needs refining.

Marking it compliant is misleading, and the other options create noise or lose data.

questions.stem: The chief compliance officer wants to see how compliant the company is with each regulation. What is the most direct view?
options: Compliance by authority document, rolled up from controls
The number of users who hold compliance-related roles
A count of the entity types configured on the instance
A list of all controls, sorted by their creation date
questions.explanation:
Authority document compliance shows each regulation's status, built from the mapping chain down to controls. That's what regulators and executives ask for.

The other views say nothing about regulatory compliance.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a risk framework in Risk Management?
options: To organize risk statements into categories, such as operational risk
To schedule audit engagements for the highest-rated risk categories
To store the approvals and rationale recorded for every accepted risk
To define which users are permitted to create and modify entities
questions.explanation:
Risk frameworks categorize the risk library, which makes reporting by category possible and keeps the library manageable.

Approvals, entity permissions, and audit scheduling are handled elsewhere.

questions.stem: What is a risk owner responsible for?
options: Managing the risk: keeping assessments current and driving the response
Approving every policy and standard published across the organization
Testing related controls independently on behalf of internal audit
Configuring the risk assessment methodologies and scoring formulas
questions.explanation:
Risk owners are accountable for their risks — assessing them, deciding and driving responses, and escalating when exposure changes.

Policy approval, independent testing, and methodology configuration belong to other roles.

questions.stem: Besides a scheduled cycle, when should a risk be reassessed?
options: After a significant event, such as a major incident or a breached KRI
Only when an internal or external auditor specifically requests it
Never; risks should only be reassessed in the scheduled annual cycle
Every time any user opens and views the risk record on the platform
questions.explanation:
