Event-driven reassessment keeps risk ratings meaningful when circumstances change. Waiting for the next cycle leaves decisions based on stale data.

Audit requests and record views aren't meaningful triggers.

questions.stem: Why should likelihood and impact scales be defined with clear criteria?
options: So the heat map shows only high risks
So assessments can be skipped for low-impact risks
So different assessors rate similar risks consistently
So every risk receives the same score
questions.explanation:
Defined criteria — for example, "major impact means losses over $1M or regulatory sanction" — make ratings comparable across assessors and business units.

The goal is consistency, not identical scores or hidden risks.

questions.stem: In advanced risk assessment, who typically participates in an assessment?
options: Only the external auditors who review the risk program each year
An assessor who completes it and an approver who confirms the result
Only the platform administrator who configured the methodology
Every employee in the business unit that owns the related entity
questions.explanation:
Assessments generally have assessors who provide ratings and approvers who validate them before results are final. That separation adds quality control.

Administrators configure, auditors stay independent, and assessing with everyone is impractical.

questions.stem: In advanced risk assessment, what is the difference between manual and automated factors?
options: There is no difference, since assessors answer both types of factor by hand
Manual factors are used only for inherent risk, automated ones only for residual risk
Automated factors must be approved by external auditors before they can be used
Manual factors are answered by assessors; automated factors pull values from data
questions.explanation:
Manual factors capture judgment through questions. Automated factors pull values from data — for example, the number of open critical vulnerabilities — which reduces subjectivity.

Either type can be used in different assessment stages, and neither requires audit approval.

questions.stem: What does a group factor do in advanced risk assessment?
options: Merges duplicate risks for the same entity into one record
Assigns the risk assessment to a group of users at once
Combines several child factors into one calculated value
Groups risks by entity class so they can be reported together
questions.explanation:
Group factors aggregate child factors — for example, combining financial, reputational, and regulatory impact into one impact score — using a defined calculation.

Assignment, reporting, and merging are separate functions.

questions.stem: A risk response plan includes deploying data loss prevention to reduce the chance of data leaking. How is this tracked?
options: As response tasks linked to the risk, with owners and due dates
As a new entity type created for the data loss prevention tool
As a citation added to the relevant privacy authority document
As a note added to the risk's description field for reference
questions.explanation:
Response tasks make the plan trackable and show progress toward target risk.

Descriptions can't be tracked, and entity types and citations serve other purposes.

questions.stem: A company decides to stop offering a product line in a high-risk market rather than manage the regulatory exposure. Which response is this?
options: Transfer
Accept
Mitigate
Avoid
questions.explanation: Ending the activity that creates the risk is avoidance. Acceptance would keep the risk, transfer would shift its consequences, and mitigation would reduce it with controls.

questions.stem: A risk acceptance reaches its expiration date. What should happen?
options: The risk is transferred to internal audit for ownership and follow-up
The risk is reviewed to renew the acceptance or choose another response
The risk is deleted, since the acceptance period has now ended
The acceptance renews automatically for another year without review
questions.explanation:
Expiry exists to force a fresh decision when circumstances may have changed.

Deleting the risk or renewing automatically defeats the purpose, and audit doesn't take ownership of risks.

questions.stem: What is the difference between risk appetite and risk tolerance?
options: Appetite is the overall risk level the organization will pursue; tolerance is acceptable variation for specific risks
Tolerance is set by regulators for each industry, while appetite is set by the external auditors
They mean exactly the same thing, and frameworks use the two terms interchangeably for the same limit
Appetite applies only to financial risks, while tolerance applies only to information technology risks
questions.explanation:
Appetite is the broad statement of how much risk the organization will take. Tolerance sets more specific acceptable ranges, which are useful as thresholds.

Neither is limited to one risk type, and both are set by the organization's leadership.

questions.stem: What is an emerging risk?
options: A new or developing risk that isn't yet well understood
A risk that has already been formally accepted and approved
The risk with the highest residual score in the register
A risk that was retired in the previous assessment cycle
questions.explanation:
Emerging risks — new technologies, regulations, or threats — are tracked early even though they're hard to quantify, so the organization isn't caught unprepared.

Status and score don't make a risk emerging.

questions.stem: A key risk indicator crosses its threshold. What is a typical configured response?
options: Delete the risk, since the indicator has already captured the problem
Notify the risk owner and create an issue or trigger a reassessment
Lower the inherent risk score automatically to offset the breach
Close all of the related controls until the indicator recovers
questions.explanation:
A breached KRI means exposure may have changed. Notifying the owner and creating follow-up work turns the signal into action.

Deleting the risk or lowering scores would hide the signal.

questions.stem: A major security incident causes financial loss. How should it connect to Risk Management?
options: Create a new policy for the incident and publish it to all employees
Record a risk event linked to the related risks and the incident
Ignore it, since incidents and risk management aren't related processes
Close the related risks, since the event they described has occurred
questions.explanation:
Linking actual loss events to risks validates or challenges current ratings and builds loss history for future assessments.

Risks remain after an event, and creating a policy per incident isn't a risk process.

questions.stem: How can a risk manager assess all risks for one entity in a single exercise?
options: Assess each risk on a different day for accuracy
Create a separate new entity for each of its risks
Export the risks and assess them in a spreadsheet
Use an assessment scope covering the entity's risks
questions.explanation:
Advanced risk assessment supports scoping assessments to an entity and its risks, so related risks are assessed consistently in one effort.

Splitting entities or moving work off-platform loses consistency and traceability.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a top-down risk assessment from a bottom-up one?
options: Top-down starts from strategic objectives; bottom-up builds up from operational risks
There is no practical difference between the two approaches in a risk program
Top-down assessments are done only by auditors, and bottom-up assessments only by IT
Top-down assessments don't use likelihood or impact ratings at any point
questions.explanation:
Top-down captures leadership's view of what threatens objectives, while bottom-up captures detailed operational risks. Mature programs use both and reconcile them.

The approaches aren't tied to particular teams, and both use likelihood and impact.

questions.stem: A database is worth $500,000, and a breach is expected to damage 40% of its value. What is the single loss expectancy?
questions.explanation: SLE = asset value × exposure factor = $500,000 × 0.40 = $200,000. Multiplying SLE by the annual rate of occurrence gives the annualized loss expectancy.

questions.stem: On a heat map, how should a risk with low likelihood but catastrophic impact generally be treated?
options: Accepted automatically, because it is unlikely to happen
Ignored, because its likelihood is low enough not to matter
Evaluated against appetite, since its impact could be severe
Treated the same as a low-likelihood, low-impact risk
questions.explanation:
Low-likelihood, high-impact risks — such as a datacenter loss — can threaten the organization even though they're rare. They need deliberate treatment, often through resilience planning.

Ignoring or automatically accepting them is how surprises happen.

questions.stem: Why link controls to the risks they mitigate?
options: So each control is reassigned to the risk owner automatically when linked
So the risk is closed automatically as soon as the control is created
Because a risk can't be assessed until it has at least ten linked controls
So control effectiveness informs residual risk and failures show their impact
questions.explanation:
The control-to-risk link connects compliance and risk: residual risk reflects how well mitigating controls work, and a control failure signals rising exposure.

The link doesn't reassign ownership, impose minimum counts, or close risks.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the risk library and the risk register?
options: The library holds reusable statements; the register holds risks identified for entities
They are the same list, viewed by different roles in the risk application
The library holds risks that have been closed; the register holds risks still open
The library is maintained for auditors, while the register is maintained for regulators
questions.explanation:
Library statements are templates. When applied to entities, they generate the risks that make up the register.

Status and audience don't distinguish them.

questions.stem: After an assessor submits a risk assessment, what typically happens next?
options: It is sent to the external auditor for a formal signature
It is published to the knowledge base for all employees
It goes to an approver, often the risk manager, for review
It is closed automatically without any further review
questions.explanation:
Review and approval validate the assessor's ratings and add a quality check before scores affect reporting.

Knowledge publishing and external sign-off aren't part of the assessment workflow.

questions.stem: Why would a risk program use qualitative assessment rather than quantitative?
options: Qualitative assessment is required by every regulation the company follows
Reliable loss data is unavailable, and a consistent relative ranking is enough
Quantitative assessment can't be configured on the ServiceNow platform at all
Qualitative assessment produces the dollar values that executives ask for
questions.explanation:
Qualitative scales are quicker and work without robust loss data, so they're common for broad risk coverage. Quantitative methods are better when monetary estimates are needed and data supports them.

Neither is universally mandated, both can be configured, and only quantitative produces currency values.

questions.stem: Vulnerability data from Security Operations shows critical findings on servers in scope for a hardening policy. How can IRM use it?
options: Nothing, because IRM can't use data from Security Operations
Create a policy exception for every vulnerability that is discovered
Use indicators or automated factors that reference the vulnerability data
Copy the vulnerabilities into the authority document as new citations
questions.explanation:
Because both run on the same platform, indicators and risk factors can reference security data directly, turning operational findings into control and risk signals.

Authority documents describe regulations, blanket exceptions hide problems, and the data is accessible.

questions.stem: What do Performance Analytics content packs add to risk and compliance?
options: Automatic approval of risk acceptances that fall within appetite
Additional entity types for common CMDB and organizational tables
Prebuilt indicators and dashboards for trends in compliance and risk
New authority documents and citations for common regulations
questions.explanation:
Content packs provide ready-made PA indicators and dashboards, so you can show trends instead of point-in-time snapshots.

They don't supply regulatory content, approve anything, or create entity types.

questions.stem: Many control owners are missing their attestation due dates. Which platform capability helps most?
options: Marking overdue attestations compliant automatically after the due date
Extending every due date by six months so owners have more time to respond
Removing due dates so control owners can respond whenever they're ready
Notifications and reminders around due dates, with escalation to managers
questions.explanation:
Reminders and escalation use standard platform notifications to drive completion without lowering standards.

Extending, auto-passing, or removing due dates hides the problem.

questions.stem: A regulatory alert arrives about a change to a privacy law. What is the first step in regulatory change management?
options: Forward the regulatory alert to all employees so they're aware of the change
Publish a new privacy policy immediately so employees learn about the change
Delete the existing authority document so the new version can replace it
Assess whether it's relevant and which documents, policies, and controls it affects
questions.explanation:
Relevance and impact assessment come first, so the right owners update the right policies and controls.

Deleting, publishing, or broadcasting before understanding the impact causes confusion.

questions.stem: How do third-party risk processes connect to the IRM data model?
options: Vendors can be entities, so third-party work uses the same framework as internal work
Vendors must be modeled as policy statements under a third-party risk policy
Third-party risk can't share any data with IRM, so it runs as a separate program
Third parties are added as citations under a vendor management authority document
questions.explanation:
Modeling vendors as entities brings third-party risk into the same reporting and issue management as the rest of the program.

Policy statements and citations describe requirements, not vendors.

questions.stem: How do business continuity and operational resilience applications build on the IRM foundation?
options: They reuse entities, risks, and issues, connecting resilience to the same data
They require a separate instance so resilience data stays isolated from IRM
They replace Policy and Compliance once resilience planning has been set up
They don't relate to IRM at all and use an entirely different data model
questions.explanation:
Resilience applications use the shared GRC data model, linking critical services and plans to the same entities and risks.

They extend rather than replace, run on the same instance, and are closely related.

questions.stem: An issue from a failed control requires a firewall change by the network team. How is the work best handled?
options: Email the network team about the change and close the issue right away
Mark the issue as accepted, since another team owns the firewall
Create remediation tasks or a related change request from the issue
Wait for the next attestation cycle to confirm the problem still exists
questions.explanation:
Linking remediation to the teams and processes that do the work — including change management — keeps the fix traceable back to the finding.

Closing on an email or accepting the risk doesn't fix anything, and waiting delays remediation.

questions.stem: How should internal audit decide which engagements to include in its annual audit plan?
options: Choose the areas with the fewest open issues so the audit finishes quickly
Prioritize by risk, using the risk and compliance data on the platform
Let each business unit decide for itself whether it will be audited this year
Audit the same areas every year, working through them in alphabetical order
questions.explanation:
Risk-based planning focuses limited audit resources where exposure is greatest, and shared IRM data makes that view available.

Fixed rotations, self-selection, and avoiding problem areas miss the point of audit.

questions.stem: In which phase of an audit engagement do auditors perform tests and gather evidence?
options: Closed
Follow-up
Scoping
Fieldwork
questions.explanation: Fieldwork is where testing and evidence gathering happen. Scoping defines what's covered, follow-up tracks remediation of findings, and closed means the engagement is complete.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a walkthrough during an audit?
options: To close all related issues once the auditors have seen the process
To create new entities for every system involved in the audited process
To review and approve the final audit report before it is distributed
To trace a process end to end and confirm how controls are performed
questions.explanation:
Walkthroughs confirm the auditor's understanding of a process and its controls before detailed testing.

Report approval, issue closure, and entity creation are separate steps.

questions.stem: How are audit results typically communicated to management?
options: They aren't communicated to management until the following audit year
Through individual emails sent to management after each test is finished
Through an audit report covering scope, observations, ratings, and actions
By publishing the raw test data and workpapers to the knowledge base
questions.explanation:
The audit report is the formal deliverable, summarizing what was examined, what was found, and what management has agreed to do.

Piecemeal emails and raw data aren't a formal communication.

questions.stem: Management says an audit issue has been remediated. What should happen before it is closed?
options: The issue is deleted so it no longer appears in open-issue reporting
The finding is reclassified as a risk acceptance so it can be closed faster
The remediation is validated, often by audit, to confirm it fixes the finding
The issue is closed immediately, based on management's confirmation alone
questions.explanation:
Validation confirms the fix actually works. Closing on assertion alone undermines the audit's assurance.

Deleting or reclassifying the issue misrepresents what happened.
